title: In the Heights
tag: The streets are made of music
why: Hamilton’s lyrical propulsion meets neighborhood-scale longing, huge ensemble energy, rhythmic movement, and songs that keep turning ordinary speech into something bigger.
risk: Long runtime with a few quieter stretches.

enrichment.notes: Strong bridge between Hamilton-style lyrical momentum and warmer neighborhood-scale musical storytelling.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Bo Burnham: Inside
tag: Existential crisis, but make it bang
why: A performer turns interior experience into spectacle. Clever construction, escalating motifs, musical jokes that become emotional gut-punches, and songs that are impossible to experience passively.
risk: Existential material can hit differently depending on mood.

friction: existential material can intensify a low mood
enrichment.notes: A key proof that “musical propulsion” can come from conceptual construction and escalation, not traditional movie-musical form.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Moulin Rouge!
why: The gold standard for emotional maximalism: familiar songs are transformed into narrative weapons, and the movie commits completely whenever emotion becomes too large for dialogue.
risk: Absolutely none if maximalism is what you came for.

enrichment.notes: Primary reference title for emotional maximalism. Familiar songs are not decoration here; they are reorganized into narrative propulsion.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Moana
why: A near-perfect blend of comfort and propulsion: irresistible hooks, identity yearning, comic release, emotional reprises, and a soundtrack that still moves even when it feels like home.
risk: None. This is a core comfort anchor.

friction: lower maximalism than the most explosive titles
enrichment.notes: Core comfort anchor. Useful because it proves comfort and propulsion are not opposites.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Hamilton
why: Proof that lyrical complexity is not a barrier when momentum is high enough. Dense callbacks, overlapping vocals, motifs, escalation, and constant musical forward motion.
risk: Caption-heavy, but you already know the engine overcomes that.

friction: caption dependence can increase cognitive load
enrichment.notes: Important counterexample to the idea that familiarity is required for singability. Momentum and emotional legibility can overcome extreme lyrical density.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: tick, tick…BOOM!
why: Creative anxiety becomes rhythm. It turns time pressure, ambition, grief, friendship, and fear into music with an almost physical sense of countdown.
risk: Existential career panic may occasionally hit home.

friction: career anxiety themes can hit personally
enrichment.notes: Turns time pressure itself into rhythm. Strong fit when urgency, creative identity, and emotional release need to arrive together.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: The Greatest Showman
tag: Pop anthems in a top hat
why: A practically industrial-strength anthem machine. The plot is less important than the repeated experience of a song finding a runway and taking off.
risk: Subtlety has left the building.

friction: narrative is less sophisticated than the soundtrack
enrichment.notes: Excellent calibration title for separating musical payoff from plot quality. The soundtrack itself carries extraordinary propulsion.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Wicked
why: Big melodic architecture, huge emotional builds, identity and belonging, and perhaps the purest possible example of a song escalating until participation becomes compulsory.
risk: Long, but the musical peaks earn it.

friction: slower dramatic passages between major numbers
enrichment.notes: High-value reference for belt instinct and maximal emotional payoff, while still carrying substantial narrative integration.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: The Phantom of the Opera
why: A perfect example of belt instinct having nothing to do with lyric familiarity. The score is physically enormous and emotion is treated as an architectural material.
risk: Melodrama is the feature.
songs: Wishing You Were Somehow Here Again

friction: Operatic vocal style can feel formal
enrichment.notes: A maximalist gothic bridge between spectacle and emotional surrender. The score is nearly continuous, which makes it feel propelled even when the plot slows.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile of musical experience and likely fit.

title: Dear Evan Hansen
why: The emotional valence can be brutal, but the melodies build toward release. “Waving Through a Window” is the canonical example of sadness becoming physically singable.
risk: Suicide and grief themes.

friction: Story discomfort may compete with soundtrack appeal
enrichment.notes: The songs often outrun the movie in replay value. Strong belt instinct and emotional amplitude make the soundtrack more propulsive than the narrative itself.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile; mood/friction notes reflect editorial judgment.

title: Across the Universe
why: Songs you know are recontextualized until they feel newly attached to story and character. It satisfies both musical recognition and the deeper pleasure of seeing music become narrative.
risk: Some dreamier passages slow the pulse.

friction: dreamlike passages slow conventional narrative momentum

gatewaySongs.song: I Want to Hold Your Hand

enrichment.notes: A major jukebox reference because familiar music is emotionally reattached to new narrative contexts rather than merely performed.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Annie
why: The childhood anchor proves “traditional Broadway” was never the problem. Hook density, emotional clarity, comic character songs, and irresistible escalation mattered from the beginning.
risk: None. The VHS already answered this question.
songs: I Think I’m Gonna Like It Here

gatewaySongs.song: I Think I’m Gonna Like It Here

enrichment.notes: Comfort-forward rather than feral, but the melody density, familiarity, and repeated ensemble payoffs make it unusually replayable.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile; familiarity advantage includes known personal nostalgia context.

title: KPop Demon Hunters
why: A clean modern example of propulsion engineering: relentless hooks, identity stakes, kinetic production, huge choruses, and emotional songs that still feel designed for bodily participation.
risk: May create involuntary replay loops.

friction: hyper-polished pop style may be too glossy for some moods
enrichment.notes: Strong evidence that immediate singability can emerge from hook density and emotional clarity without prior familiarity.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: O’Dessa
why: It commits. Rock-opera theatricality, neon maximalism, big emotions, and songs that act like the fuel source for the entire strange world.
risk: Deliberately weird and stylized.

enrichment.notes: Its value is less conventional musical-theater structure and more total aesthetic commitment: rock mythology, heightened emotion, and stylized momentum.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile based on engine framing and catalog scoring.

title: Walk the Line
why: The music hits hardest because story, performance, desire, and character converge inside the songs. Less “musical,” but very strong music-as-emotional-language evidence.
risk: More performance-driven than reality-breaking musical.

friction: less wall-to-wall musical than traditional musicals
enrichment.notes: Critical musical-adjacent reference. Demonstrates that performance scenes can provide propulsion even when the film itself is not structurally a musical.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Dr. Horrible’s Sing-Along Blog
why: Short-form proof that cleverness and emotional propulsion can coexist. Songs are plot mechanisms, jokes, character psychology, and eventually knives.
risk: The tonal turn is part of the experience.

friction: Comedy tone may mask emotional turn
enrichment.notes: Extremely efficient musical storytelling. Dense callbacks, short runtime, and escalating motif reuse create high propulsion with very little dead space.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile of structure and emotional arc.

title: Once
why: You appreciate it, but it establishes the lower boundary: beautiful music is not enough when you specifically want propulsion.
risk: Too slow for a propulsion night.

enrichment.notes: A useful counterexample in the engine: musically sincere and emotionally resonant without relying on maximalism or body movement.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile, especially useful as a low-propulsion contrast case.

title: Begin Again
why: A useful separate category: music-centered and genuinely enjoyable, but not what your brain reaches for when it wants to be musically propelled.
risk: Wrong lane if you want lift-off.
songs: Tell Me If You Wanna Go Home
A Step You Can’t Take Back

gatewaySongs.song: Tell Me If You Wanna Go Home
A Step You Can’t Take Back

enrichment.notes: Musical-adjacent by design. Best treated as a relaxed creativity-and-connection film, not a propulsion-first musical.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile preserving the distinction between musical-adjacent and full musical.

title: La La Land
why: A strategically useful negative signal: polished craft and musical prestige do not compensate for a lower level of visceral musical ignition.
risk: You already tried it; no need to force chemistry.

friction: Lower belt density and more restrained propulsion than the engine’s strongest matches
enrichment.notes: Visually and musically elegant, but its lighter vocal attack and dreamlike pacing make it a useful contrast title.

title: Dreamgirls
why: Musically a very strong fit, but personal emotional associations currently outweigh recommendation fit. The engine preserves that distinction.
risk: Currently connected to an emotional part of your upbringing you do not want to revisit.
songs: And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going

friction: Heavy interpersonal betrayal and emotionally loaded material

gatewaySongs.song: And I Am Telling You I’m Not Going

enrichment.notes: A vocal-performance engine with enormous emotional peaks, but the story material can make it context-sensitive.

title: Rocketman
tag: Elton deserves a better viewing condition
why: Unlike a conventional biopic, Elton’s songs repeatedly replace realism and become the storytelling language. Your first viewing conditions may have hidden a strong structural match.
risk: Addiction, family trauma, and darker emotional material.

friction: Narrative framing may interrupt sing-along flow
enrichment.notes: Works best when treated as fantasy-musical biography rather than literal biography. Existing attachment to Elton John substantially raises familiarity advantage.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile; familiarity advantage reflects known user affinity.

title: Bohemian Rhapsody
tag: One arena scene did a lot of work
why: The Live Aid climax delivers the arena-scale participation you love, but the surrounding movie does not consistently turn music into narrative propulsion.
risk: The teeth have historically competed for your attention.

enrichment.notes: The strongest engine fit is concentrated in performance sequences rather than the whole film. Excellent example of a title whose climax scores much higher than its average runtime.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile; friction includes previously stated viewing reaction.

title: Everybody’s Talking About Jamie
tag: Pop confidence with glitter and heart
why: Pop-forward songs, identity stakes, humor, emotional release, and a strong “spotlight” instinct make this a compelling bridge between modern musical theater and pure feel-it-in-your-body participation.
risk: Contains bullying and one heavier queer-history sequence.
songs: And You Don’t Even Know It

friction: Coming-of-age framing may feel lighter than the emotional themes underneath
enrichment.notes: A buoyant pop-musical with real emotional stakes, strongest when self-definition becomes anthem.

title: Hedwig and the Angry Inch
why: The Inside + O’Dessa + Moulin Rouge intersection: persona, performance, pain, rock theatricality, and music used to construct and deconstruct identity in real time.
risk: Sexual content, identity trauma, emotional rough edges.

friction: Angular tone and deliberately abrasive character work
enrichment.notes: Cult rock musical where identity, performance, and emotional rupture are fused into the songs.

title: Rent
tag: Rock musical feelings at emergency volume
why: Rock-forward hooks, ensemble urgency, characters wanting things desperately, and emotional escalation. A strong fit if heavier subject matter is welcome.
risk: AIDS, death, addiction, grief.

enrichment.notes: High narrative integration and emotional amplitude. It should connect strongly to tick, tick…BOOM! while feeling more ensemble-driven and less tightly paced.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile of musical and emotional mechanics.

title: Jesus Christ Superstar
tag: A rock opera with no chill
why: It is basically continuous musical argument. Massive voices, riff-driven urgency, theological/existential conflict, and almost no conventional dialogue to interrupt the engine.
risk: Very 1970s visual language; spiritually intense subject matter.
songs: I Don’t Know How to Love Him

enrichment.notes: One of the purest propulsion cases in the catalog because almost nothing is outside the score. High lyrical density plus rock-opera continuity creates relentless forward motion.

provenance.note: Interpretive profile; useful as a sung-through benchmark.

title: Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit
why: Choir music is essentially engineered participation. Gospel call-and-response, huge ensemble lift, Lauryn Hill, and finales that refuse to let the body remain neutral.
risk: Low stakes, which may be exactly the point.
songs: His Eye Is on the Sparrow

enrichment.notes: Not continuous-musical storytelling, but performance peaks are extraordinary on belt, body movement, communal joy, and catharsis.

title: The Color Purple
tag: Hard-earned catharsis in gospel and soul
why: The emotional amplitude is enormous and the score offers powerful release, especially if you want to be moved rather than kept emotionally safe.
risk: Abuse, trauma, racism, and heavy subject matter.

friction: Trauma-heavy story and intense emotional subject matter
enrichment.notes: A deeply emotional gospel-and-soul musical whose payoff is enormous when the viewer has capacity for the story.

title: Hairspray
why: Almost laboratory-perfect for musical propulsion: immediate hooks, movement, comic character songs, soul influence, and an ending engineered to make sitting still impossible.
risk: None if joy is the assignment.

enrichment.notes: One of the clearest joy-propulsion titles in the catalog. Especially valuable for body movement, communal lift, and replay value.

provenance.source: Musical Propulsion Engine core enrichment batch v1

title: Encanto
tag: Lin-Manuel hooks in a magical pressure cooker
why: The Moana/Hamilton bridge in its purest form: layered lyrics, memorable hooks, family dynamics, rhythmic momentum, and songs that expose internal pressure rather than pause the story.
risk: Family dynamics may be more emotional than the bright palette suggests.

friction: Family-pressure themes can hit harder than the bright surface suggests
enrichment.notes: Dense character writing and hooks disguised as family animation, with strong replay and comfort value.

title: Sing Street
why: Less maximal than your core anchors, but stronger propulsion than Once or Begin Again. Original songs are catchy enough to become emotional shortcuts quickly.
risk: More music-centered coming-of-age film than full reality-breaking musical.
songs: Drive It Like You Stole It

friction: Less sung-through than a traditional musical

gatewaySongs.song: Drive It Like You Stole It

enrichment.notes: Musical-adjacent in structure but highly propulsive when creativity and escape take over.

title: West Side Story
why: Evidence that “traditional Broadway” is not disqualifying when cinematic momentum, movement, longing, and musical escalation are operating at full force.
risk: Tragic outcome and long runtime.
songs: A Boy Like That / I Have a Love

friction: Tragic ending and heavier dramatic material

gatewaySongs.song: A Boy Like That / I Have a Love

enrichment.notes: A full-scale cinematic musical with enormous movement and emotional amplitude despite a more traditional score profile.

title: Little Shop of Horrors
tag: Motown hooks plus a carnivorous plant
why: Character songs move plot at speed, the Motown/do-wop vocabulary is immediately hooky, and the tonal escalation is delightfully unhinged.
risk: Dark comedy and camp horror.
songs: Mean Green Mother from Outer Space

friction: Macabre humor and intentionally theatrical camp
enrichment.notes: Compact, hook-heavy, weird, and extremely singable. A valuable camp/maximalism anchor.

title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
why: Audience participation is embedded in its cultural DNA. Glam-rock hooks, camp maximalism, and unapologetic theatricality are very strong propulsion signals.
risk: 1970s sexual politics and deliberate camp weirdness.

friction: Deliberately chaotic tone and dated transgressive humor
enrichment.notes: Less emotional propulsion than some anchors, but exceptional communal singability, camp, and body-movement value.

title: Sweeney Todd
why: Not upbeat, but emotionally and structurally relentless. Motifs recur like intrusive thoughts and the score rarely stops functioning as narrative machinery.
risk: Graphic violence, murder, bleakness.

friction: Bleak violence, low comfort, and deliberately grim atmosphere
enrichment.notes: A dense, nearly continuous score with maximal narrative integration, but comfort is intentionally near zero.

title: The Last Five Years
why: Less kinetic, but structurally clever and emotionally intense. Best when you want huge feelings and vocal catharsis more than movement.
risk: Relationship breakdown is the entire architecture.

friction: Emotionally bruising relationship structure and limited ensemble lift
enrichment.notes: Almost entirely sung and emotionally direct. High narrative integration, lower communal/ensemble energy.

title: Spirited
why: Huge choreography, aggressive commitment, comic escalation, and several songs built to become full-body events.
risk: Holiday framing and broad comedy may be mood-dependent.

enrichment.notes: A strong maximalist test case where choreography and comic escalation do much of the propulsion work.

title: Matilda the Musical
why: Sharp lyrical storytelling, giant ensemble choreography, emotional cruelty-to-catharsis arcs, and a spectacular release valve in Revolting Children.
risk: Its deliberately grotesque adults and child-abuse themes make the comfort level deceptive.

enrichment.notes: Excellent bridge between family-musical accessibility and surprisingly dark emotional architecture.

title: The Prom
why: Unapologetically theatrical, belt-heavy, bright, campy, and built around large-scale musical release.
risk: The celebrity satire and tonal broadness can feel synthetic.

enrichment.notes: Useful high-maximalism title that tests whether sheer theatrical commitment can overcome tonal unevenness.

title: Cyrano
why: Music functions as emotional confession, with aching repetition and a romantic-tragic arc that keeps tightening.
risk: Lower movement and a deliberately mournful register make it a mood-specific recommendation.

enrichment.notes: Expands the database toward restrained propulsion driven by yearning rather than spectacle.

title: Wonka
why: Buoyant melody, storybook momentum, visual invention, and a comfort-forward tone with enough musical movement to stay airborne.
risk: Lower emotional amplitude and belt intensity than the engine’s strongest anchors.
songs: You’ve Never Had Chocolate Like This

gatewaySongs.song: You’ve Never Had Chocolate Like This

enrichment.notes: A useful comfort-heavy benchmark where charm matters more than cathartic force.

title: Mean Girls
why: Modern pop production, sharp character songs, choreography, and a pace that rarely lets the musical energy fully drop.
risk: Some adaptation choices flatten the stage score and emotional peaks.

friction: glossy production can mute theatrical bite
enrichment.notes: Adds contemporary glossy pop-musical texture and a useful mid-emotion/high-movement profile.

title: Newsies: The Broadway Musical
why: Big ensemble vocals, athletic choreography, rally-song architecture, and constant communal forward motion.
risk: Stage-capture presentation may feel less cinematic.

enrichment.notes: A high-value stage-capture addition with unusually strong movement and communal propulsion.

title: Come From Away
why: Near-continuous ensemble storytelling turns logistical chaos into rhythmic propulsion, then lands enormous communal catharsis.
risk: Subject matter around 9/11 can make the emotional load heavier than the warmth suggests.
songs: Somewhere in the Middle of Nowhere

enrichment.notes: Crucial evidence that maximalism is not required for extreme propulsion when ensemble narrative density is high.

title: Shrek the Musical
tag: Fairytale camp with a giant heart
why: Broad comedy and theatrical excess hide a surprisingly sincere outsider story with strong belt moments and ensemble payoff.
risk: Some humor is intentionally juvenile and the filmed-stage aesthetic is broad.

enrichment.notes: Adds camp-forward stage musical energy with genuine emotional payoff.

title: Rock of Ages
why: Familiar arena-rock hooks, huge vocals, shameless mashups, and maximalist commitment make narrative subtlety almost irrelevant.
risk: Thin story and deliberately trashy tone.

enrichment.notes: A useful stress test for how far hook familiarity and belt energy can carry a weak narrative.

title: Purple Rain
why: The performance sequences are overwhelming musical events, with hooks and charisma doing more propulsion work than the dramatic connective tissue.
risk: The offstage relationship material is darker and rougher than the concert highs.

enrichment.notes: Expands the musical-adjacent category where performance sequences create the propulsion rather than integrated song dialogue.

title: Hair
why: Communal rock hooks, physical movement, and counterculture energy create a loose but infectious musical current.
risk: Loose episodic structure and period politics may create distance.

enrichment.notes: Adds a looser counterculture-rock form with high communal energy but less narrative integration.

title: Tommy
why: Almost continuous rock storytelling, iconic hooks, visual insanity, and total commitment to a concept-album universe.
risk: Disturbing material, grotesque imagery, and aggressively strange filmmaking.

enrichment.notes: A deliberate wild-card anchor for maximalism, rock-opera continuity, and high-strangeness tolerance.

title: Blinded by the Light
why: Songs become identity language and emotional release, with familiar rock lyrics externalizing what the protagonist cannot yet say.
risk: Less fully musical than the core catalog and more dependent on connection to Springsteen’s songs.

enrichment.notes: Useful musical-adjacent case where preexisting songs become explicit narrative and identity machinery.

title: Yesterday
why: An absurdly strong songbook supplies instant hooks and comfort while the story uses musical recognition as its central emotional engine.
risk: More rom-com with performances than integrated musical.

enrichment.notes: Provides a low-integration/high-hook benchmark and a direct contrast with Across the Universe’s transformation of the same songbook.
